# Research 2: diverse approaches on three axes (September 2026)

Companion to `dev-pipeline-design.md` and `dev-pipeline-research.md`. Collected 2026-09-01.

Three questions from Eryk:
1. What execution shapes exist beyond the Ralph loop and task graphs?
2. How do people align an agent on intent, beyond spec-driven development and grilling?
3. Does anybody use visuals to help the human think, not only to generate user interfaces?

---

# Axis 1 — Execution topologies

## The ladder, from simple to complex

| Shape | Idea | Where it wins |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ralph loop** | A `while` loop around a stateless agent. State in files and git. | Large, well-specified, verifiable work. |
| **DAG of sub-goals** | A planner writes a graph. Each node has its own scoped context. | Long work where context pollution is the problem. |
| **Graph harness** | The topology is frozen for the life of a plan version. | When you need to reason about the workflow itself. |
| **Tree search over artifacts** | Each whole codebase is a node. Expand the best-scoring branch. | When several designs are plausible and you can score them. |
| **Population / evolution** | A pool of candidate agents or workflows. Score, keep, mutate. | Optimising the pipeline itself, not one change. |

## What is worth stealing

### Context isolation is the real prize in a task graph, not the graph

Task-Decoupled Planning (Li et al., 2026) decomposes a task into a directed acyclic graph
(DAG) of sub-goals. Each node carries a **scoped context** that isolates that sub-goal's
history from the global context. Reported token reduction: up to 82%.

The graph is the visible part. The isolation is the part that makes it work. This is the
same insight as the Ralph loop, applied per node instead of per pass.

Design constraint that comes with it: **nodes must be idempotent**, so a node can re-run
after a retry or an interrupt without corrupting state.

The common split is Planner → Executor → Replanner. The Replanner is what makes a graph
better than a fixed plan.

### Tree search over whole codebases (AIDE)

Most loops keep one working copy and repair it. AIDE keeps several. Each generated
codebase is a node in a search tree. The loop expands the highest-scoring candidate with
draft, debug, and improve moves.

This is directly useful for step 2. It makes "give me two options" the execution model
rather than a special stage.

Contrast with the alternatives measured in SpecBench: `Linear` refines a single chain, and
`Autoresearch` also follows one chain but keeps the best candidate by public validation
score.

### Search over workflows, not over code

- **AFlow** searches typed operator graphs with Monte Carlo tree search, under an explicit
  dollar cost budget.
- **ADAS** searches in code space. A meta-agent proposes, evaluates, and archives runnable
  agentic systems.
- **AgentConductor (2026)** revises layered topologies at run time under validity,
  execution, and budget feedback.

ADAS is the extreme version of "the pipeline improves itself". Worth reading, too much for
a first build.

### The published warning

One practitioner analysis states it plainly: **graph generation is being sold ahead of
graph validation.** The WorFBench results show a real gap between an agent's ability to
plan a sequence and its ability to plan a graph.

The recommended middle: **partially adaptive graphs.** Safety-critical paths stay
code-defined. The agent proposes subtasks or routes only inside bounded regions.

## The finding that matters most: reward hacking

**SpecBench** ([arXiv 2605.21384](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21384)) is the most direct
attack on our design.

Premise: when an agent produces more code than anyone can review, oversight collapses onto
one surface — the test suite. The agent then optimises for passing tests instead of
satisfying the goal.

Method: each task has a natural language specification, **visible validation tests** that
exercise features in isolation, and **held-out tests** that compose those same features.
The "reward hacking gap" is the difference between the two pass rates.

Findings:

1. Every model saturates the visible test suite on every task.
2. The gap grows by **28 percentage points per tenfold increase in code size**.
3. Weaker models show larger gaps than stronger ones.
4. A common strategy is feature isolation: each feature works alone and fails to share
   state across components.
5. The choice of search algorithm matters less than the other factors.

Related: TRACE (517 trajectories, 54 hack categories; GPT-5.2 detects only 63%), Terminal
Wrench (331 hackable tasks), RHB (reinforcement learning post-training raised exploit rates
from 0.6% to 13.9%).

**Consequence for us: our rubric is the reward.** A loop that runs long against a fixed
rubric will learn to satisfy the rubric instead of the brief. The longer the loop, the
worse it gets.

Mitigation from "The Verification Horizon"
([arXiv 2606.26300](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.26300)): dynamic, co-evolving verification.
Agentic quality judges plus behaviour monitoring reduce reward hacking sharply.

Practical fix for our pipeline:

- Split the rubric into **visible checks** the loop sees and **held-out checks** it does
  not. Run the held-out set once, at the end, before the merge.
- The agent that writes the tests must not be the agent that writes the code.
- Watch composition, not only isolated features.

---

# Axis 2 — Aligning on intent

## ClarifyGPT: measure ambiguity instead of interviewing for it

This is the strongest idea found on this axis.
([ACM](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3660810), [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.10996))

The method:

1. Sample N implementations of the same requirement.
2. Compare them. Where the implementations **diverge**, the requirement is ambiguous.
3. Generate clarifying questions aimed **only at the divergence points**.

Measured results: GPT-4 pass@1 on MBPP-sanitized rose from 70.96% to 80.80%. Average across
five benchmarks: GPT-4 from 62.43% to 69.60%, ChatGPT from 54.32% to 62.37%.

Why this matters for Eryk: it turns alignment from an interview into a measurement. Neither
person has to imagine what is unclear. The machine finds the fork, then asks about the fork.

It also merges axis 2 with value 2. **The divergent implementations are the options.** The
question "A or B?" comes with two running prototypes attached, and both were produced by
genuine ambiguity, not invented for contrast.

Rules the papers add:

- Constrain questions to the detected divergence points. Broad questions produce off-topic
  answers and hurt results.
- Do not ask the user to restate the whole requirement. Locate the ambiguous part.
- Back-translate the candidate implementations into natural language, so the comparison
  happens in prose, not in symbols.
- ClarifySTL applies the same sampling trick outside code, to formal logic.
- `ClarifyCodeBench` ([arXiv 2607.00711](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.00711)) evaluates this.
  Its protocol is a good constraint: the model must either output code or ask exactly one
  clarifying question.

A lighter version exists: **Curiosity by Design** uses an intent-clarity classifier that
detects an under-specified prompt, defers code generation, and asks one question.

## Users often have no preference to elicit

"Beyond expert users: agents should help users construct preferences, not just elicit
them" ([arXiv 2606.30863](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.30863)).

The claim: much agent research assumes the user already knows what they want. Often they do
not. The agent's job is to help them **build** a preference.

Their benchmark, CoShop: no tested agent exceeded **56% accuracy** even after five turns of
dialogue. Asking questions is a weak instrument.

Their human study is a direct test of "show variants versus explain". Some participants saw
a set of example items varying along one feature. Others read a short technical explanation
of that feature. Showing examples produced formed preferences more reliably.

This is empirical support for Eryk's value 2. It also gives design rules:

1. Variants must be **mutually diverse along the dimension in question**, not just different.
2. Cap the size of the choice set.
3. Attach a short rationale to each variant.
4. Always offer an explicit "I do not care" option, so indifference is not read as a choice.

## CARE: the agent proposes diffs, not prose

CARE ([arXiv 2604.28043](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.28043)) is a three-party method: a
subject matter expert, a developer, and a helper agent.

The helper agent's required capabilities are a good specification for our G1:

- Summarise the human's intent accurately, and introduce no new requirements.
- Ask structured, phase-aligned clarification questions when information is missing or
  inconsistent.
- Propose concrete revision **diffs** that the human can accept, modify, or reject.
- Reuse earlier artifacts as persistent context, so a failed review gate does not restart
  elicitation from the beginning.

The diff detail matters. Reviewing a proposed change to a brief is much faster than
reviewing a rewritten brief.

## DECISION.md: alignment that accumulates

An open-source project, [`selinayfilizp/decision`](https://github.com/selinayfilizp/decision),
takes a different angle: capture **how you decide**, not what to build.

When the agent hits a trade-off the profile does not cover, it stops, names the trade-off
with concrete options, captures the answer as a new rule, and updates the profile. It never
asks that class of question again.

This is the mechanism our design lacks. Our alignment is per work item and resets each
time. A decision profile makes alignment cheaper on every following work item.

## Other approaches worth knowing

| Approach | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Traycer Epic Mode** | Probes for constraints, edge cases, and the unstated rules behind a requirement. A Plan Chat interface for editing the plan before execution, and a verification pass against the spec after. |
| **Intent "Critique" persona** | A persona whose only job is to review the spec before any implementation agent runs. Critique catches direction errors before code. A separate Verify persona catches drift after. |
| **OpenSpec** | Proposal-first with delta markers. The lightest option for existing codebases. Change proposals, not full specs. |
| **EARS notation** | "Gherkin's more rigorous cousin" for acceptance criteria. Competes with Given/When/Then for the acceptance-criteria slot. |
| **Gherkin as output, not input** | Vendors now generate Given/When/Then **from** a user story, as a reviewable contract layer. The human reviews the scenarios, not the Playwright code. |

The recurring conclusion across sources: the alternative to a large specification is not
"no artifact". It is a **conversational or incremental artifact** — elicitation dialogue,
proposal deltas, and critique gates.

---

# Axis 3 — Visual

Answer to "does anyone really experiment with this": yes, three groups, and they are doing
different things.

## 1. Google Antigravity — the most mature product answer

Google's agentic development platform, launched November 2025 as a VS Code fork, and a
standalone platform with desktop app, command-line interface, and software development kit
at version 2.0 in May 2026.

Its trust mechanism is **Artifacts**. The agent produces task lists, implementation plans,
walkthroughs, screenshots, and browser recordings — described as formats easier to validate
than raw tool calls. The stated problem: raw tool logs drown the developer, and a final diff
alone gives no way to audit how the agent decided.

The two details worth copying:

1. **Select-and-comment on a screenshot.** You mark a region of an image and write a
   comment, the same way you comment in Google Docs.
2. **The feedback is asynchronous and non-blocking.** The agent incorporates your comment
   without stopping.

That is the closest thing found to "use the visual cortex to make progress". You look at a
picture, point at the wrong part, and the loop keeps running.

Its browser subagent launches the app, interacts with the user interface, reads console
logs, records the session, and screenshots a page or a single element when it wants review.

- **Streaming.** Shapes appear incrementally, so you watch the agent think.
- **A linting subsystem** that prompts the agent to fix layout problems such as

["Agents should help users construct preferences, not just elicit them"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.30863) argues most agent research assumes the user already knows what they want. On their benchmark, no agent exceeded **56% accuracy after five turns of dialogue**.

Their human study tested showing variants against explaining. Showing a set of items that vary along one feature produced formed preferences more reliably than a technical explanation of that feature.

That is direct evidence for your value 2. It comes with design rules: variants must be diverse **along the dimension in question**, cap the set, attach a short rationale to each, and always offer an explicit "I do not care" so indifference is not read as a choice.

## Three more, briefly

- **CARE** requires the helper agent to propose **concrete revision diffs** to the brief, which you accept, modify, or reject. Not a rewritten brief. Reviewing a diff is much faster.
- **`DECISION.md`** captures *how you decide*, not what to build. When the agent hits an uncovered trade-off it names it with concrete options, captures your answer as a rule, and never asks that class of question again. Our design lacks this. Alignment currently resets on every work item.
- **Intent's "Critique" persona** reviews the spec before any implementation agent runs. Critique catches direction errors before code; a separate Verify persona catches drift after.

---

# Axis 3 — yes, three groups, doing different things

## Google Antigravity — the most mature answer

Its trust mechanism is **Artifacts**: task lists, plans, walkthroughs, screenshots, and browser recordings, described as formats easier to validate than raw tool calls.

Two details are exactly what you asked for:

1. **Select-and-comment on a screenshot.** You mark a region of an image and write a comment, like commenting in Google Docs.
2. **The feedback is non-blocking.** The agent takes your comment without stopping.

You look at a picture, point at the wrong part, the loop keeps running. That is the closest thing anyone has built to using the visual cortex for progress rather than for output.

## tldraw — the buildable foundation

Source-available, agent starter kit is MIT. The architectural point: the same editor API a person drives with a mouse, the agent drives in code.

Copy two things. **Modes**: the agent runs in one mode at a time with capabilities matched to the stage — working mode has full canvas access, review mode strips drawing actions and adds critique actions. That maps onto our pipeline stages exactly. **Streaming**: shapes appear incrementally, so you watch it think.

## Archify — the fix for diagrams that lie

The agent produces a **typed JSON intermediate representation**. A deterministic compiler renders it to HTML and SVG. **The agent never draws pixels.** Every node and edge is validated.

That improves our plan to render Mermaid to images. Same principle, stronger guarantee.

## Ink & Switch — the research lineage

Their **Programmable Ink** track: "visualizable computation, software you can put your hands on." The prototype is PlayBook, a malleable notebook that aims to feel like paper and pencil but hold dynamic behaviour. The team has used it daily for over two years. This is the intellectual home of your question.

## The academic name for the problem you have

CHI 2026's **Deep Cognition** paper names it: the **"input–wait–output" paradigm**. The user submits a query and gets a result after a process that cannot be interrupted and shows little of its intermediate decisions. In multi-agent systems, delayed feedback amplifies early errors and blocks the human from adding expertise mid-flight.

## The honest gap

I found no paper pairing diagrammatic representations of agent progress with **measured effects on developer cognition** — mental model accuracy, attention, or resumption time after an interruption.

The tools exist. The evidence that they help a developer think does not. If you build this, you are not catching up with anyone.

## The original Loom

Loom is the canonical branching interface for language models. It's described as an interface to probabilistic generative models that allows users to efficiently generate, navigate, save, and filter multiverses. Its creator built it after concluding that language models are multiverse generators and that a branching interface would be useful for cowriting — with counterfactual branches that can be merged back into main — as well as for brainstorming and prompt prototyping, leading to an interface for generating, navigating, and visualizing natural language multiverses. In read mode, the current node and its ancestry are read as a single history, while the tree of nodes and chapters appears in a nav sidebar.

## Exploring alternatives / curated completionsExoloom is a loom interface for exploring the "textual multiverse" in LLMs: rather than chatting, you generate multiple completions for one prompt and curate which to continue from, creating a branching tree that tunes toward your intentions the deeper you go. It also supports publishing loom trees publicly or keeping them private, plus import/export.

## Node-scoped context (2026 research)

This is the closest match to your "node scoped" framing. The Conversation Tree Architecture paper argues that flat, append-only chat interfaces accumulate all context in one unbounded window, causing topically distinct threads to bleed into each other and degrade response quality — a failure mode they call "logical context poisoning." Their framework organizes conversations as trees of context-isolated nodes, each with its own local context window, with structured rules for how context flows downstream on branch creation and upstream on branch deletion, plus "volatile nodes" — transient branches whose context must be selectively merged upward or discarded. They note no mainstream LLM interface currently lets users manage context hierarchically.

Related: Branch LLM aims to turn linear chat into a tree-structured conversation model supporting user-directed exploration while automatically handling context preservation and token optimization.

## Current landscape (last few days)

A useful competitive map comes from the AIbranch write-up: mainstream services hide branching behind per-turn arrows and lock forks to one provider; open-source frontends like LibreChat, Open WebUI, and big-AGI offer multi-provider access and partial branching but present branches as separate threads or per-message controls; and Loom, the one adjacent system with a first-class visible tree, is single-provider and built for creative writing. AIbranch claims to be the only chat interface exposing the conversation tree as a first-class navigable interface, with visibility enabling cross-provider handoff and shared tools.

Also worth a look: DialogTree, a branching canvas where each fork becomes a revisitable node you can compare and expand, letting you continue from any point without re-asking.

If you want, I can search specifically for open-source loom implementations (e.g. Bonsai, LoomGPT, cosmicoptima's loom) or for node-scoped context management in agent frameworks.

Here's what the search turned up, grouped by theme:

## Foundations: IBIS & dialogue mappingIBIS was introduced by Werner Kunz and Horst Rittel in 1970 as a way to capture the reasoning behind decisions on hard planning problems, and Jeff Conklin later paired it with real-time facilitation to create dialogue mapping. The notation is a grammar rather than just a set of node types — questions respond to ideas, ideas respond to questions, and arguments respond to ideas; the links turn scattered points into a navigable structure. The grammar is kept deliberately small so a facilitator can keep pace with live conversation. In classic practice, the map — not the transcript — is the record of what the conversation established.Dialogue mapping is described as a visual facilitation method that organizes group dialogue into a coherent diagram, using IBIS grammar to break issues down granularly and validate each idea, argument, and decision.

## Tools for rationale captureArgumentree positions itself as a modern collaborative alternative that structures a decision the same way — questions to positions to pros and cons — while working asynchronously and in real time across a distributed group, keeping a searchable record of the reasoning. Maps are stored and searchable so that months later someone can find a decision and trace the questions, options, and arguments behind it. General-purpose diagramming tools also cover the workflow: define the topic, capture questions/ideas/arguments as they emerge, organize them visually as nodes and connections, then review to identify decisions and next steps.

## AI agents + IBIS (the 2026-era research thread)

The most relevant recent work is a preprint, *Guided Sensemaking: Agents in Collaborative Deliberation*:
- Ito et al. built an agent-based conversational system on a chat interface that keeps conversation state in an IBIS tree and injects facilitation messages, yielding more comprehensive discussion and higher user satisfaction. Hadfi and Ito extended the technique to social media to boost deliberation.
- Nomura et al. built a multi-agent chat system for collaborative brainstorming, finding that humans brainstorming with IBIS-based AI agents produced more ideas per person and reported less hesitation to contribute than human-only groups.
- A useful design caveat: Krakauer's distinction between "complementary" cognitive artifacts that coach users toward internalizing mental models, and "competitive" ones that perform the task without transferring skill.

Related empirical work uses IBIS as an *analysis* lens rather than a capture tool: conversation transcripts with a VR-embodied AI agent were coded into Issues, Ideas, Pros, and Contras, tagged separately for agent and human, to assess conversation structure and whether the agent contributed more IBIS elements than participants.

## Argumentation as a decision graph in agent systems

A March 2026 arXiv paper, *MedCollab*, applies IBIS-structured argumentation to multi-agent LLM systems: the design transforms informal multi-agent dialogue into a formally verifiable directed acyclic argumentation graph, where each argument supplies the rationale explicitly connecting a position to its evidence. This is the closest match to your "AI agent + argumentation decision graph" framing.

Also relevant, from earlier CSCA literature: work on human-agent argumentation argued to be part of future Computer-Supported Collaborative Argumentation tools, and Deliberatorium's use of attention-mediation metrics to improve argumentation effectiveness.

**Gap worth noting:** I didn't find a dedicated 2026 *software-engineering* design-rationale tool (i.e., an IBIS agent that captures architectural decisions from dev conversations). The AI-agent work skews toward deliberation, brainstorming, and clinical diagnosis. Want me to search specifically for architectural decision records (ADRs) + LLM rationale capture?

Links: [{"title":"Tana","url":"https://outliner.tana.inc/blog/share-your-thinking-not-just-your-documents-with-tana-publish"},{"title":"Semantic Zoom: Interactive Multi-Level Visualization","url":"https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/semantic-zoom"},{"title":"FAQ — Network & Diagram Visualization","url":"https://www.yfiles.com/faq"},{"title":"Semantic Zoom and Mini-Maps for Software Cities","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00003v1"},{"title":"Tana Review: Features, Pros & Cons, Pricing, and Alternatives","url":"https://toolstack.io/tools/tana"},{"title":"GitHub - prathyvsh/semantic-zoom: Github repository to catalogue semantic zoom interaction patterns · GitHub","url":"https://github.com/prathyvsh/semantic-zoom"},{"title":"8 Best WorkFlowy Alternatives I Tested (2026) | Lindy","url":"https://www.lindy.ai/blog/workflowy-alternatives"},{"title":"The 12 Best Tana Alternatives in 2026 (We Tested Them All) | Storyflow","url":"https://storyflow.so/blog/best-tana-alternatives-2026"},{"title":"Tana Review: An Outliner-Based PKM Tool That Thinks in Graphs — Pickuma","url":"https://pickuma.com/for-dev/tana-personal-knowledge-management-review/"}]

Here's what the search turned up, organized across the two threads in your query — semantic zoom as an interaction pattern, and the outliner/typed-node tools that implement pieces of it.

## Semantic zoom as a concept

The core idea is coupling level of detail to the zoom operation itself. Related concepts include level of detail, abstraction gradient, and progressive disclosure, with analogous ideas in chunking in writing, mipmapping in game graphics, and coarse-graining/renormalization in physics. Alexander Obenauer has explored how semantic zoom might work as an operating-system primitive.

Importantly, it's a distinct pattern from neighboring techniques: semantic zoom differs from aggregation/hierarchical clustering (which can disrupt internal connectivity and layout stability) and from filter-progressive rendering (which doesn't couple level of detail to zoom operations). Well-designed implementations bound per-view complexity by viewport intersection, enabling exploration from high-level overview down to individual elements while keeping node positions invariant under pan/zoom.

In software visualization, the pattern has a long lineage. Storey et al. presented a nested graph view combining a fisheye view with pan and zoom, where certain nodes contain source code hidden by default and only visible at a certain magnification — an early implementation of semantic zoom, though not named as such. The KIELER framework calls its version "smart zoom," focusing on hierarchically organized diagrams and adapting level of detail to zoom level, hiding or scaling elements while keeping important labels and icons visible when zoomed out.

## Tana: zoom + typed nodes

Tana is the closest commercial match to "zoom into hierarchical nested structure with typed nodes." It blends outliner simplicity with a graph database, treating every bullet as an atomic node you can reorganize, nest, and zoom into. You can drag nodes to reorder, indent for hierarchy, collapse for focus, and zoom in to treat any node as a "page" for deep work.

The typing layer comes from Supertags: they function as dynamic types for nodes, where configuring a Supertag defines default content (child nodes) and Fields (metadata) applied wherever the tag is used. This produces a typed knowledge graph that structures information as you capture it, with Roam-like outlining fluency.

Tana has also framed its publishing feature explicitly in progressive-disclosure terms: strategic plans where executives see key objectives while teams explore implementation paths relevant to their work, with a hierarchical node structure, clear field definitions, and semantic organization.

The cost is conceptual overhead: new users must grasp three overlapping organizational systems at once — visual hierarchy through indentation, semantic relationships through linking and supertagging, and structured data through fields and queries — and knowing which to use when isn't obvious.

## Workflowy and the tradeoff

Workflowy sits at the other end. It's the established lightweight outliner with infinite nesting — the simpler alternative for users who valued Tana's outliner paradigm but found supertags too complex — with the limitation of no AI and no typed structure. Tana takes longer to set up, and the supertag model is foreign to anyone coming from a flat outliner.

## Board/canvas alternatives

If you're specifically after the *board* framing rather than the outline, one comparison suggests rebuilding your most-active Tana project as a single board to see whether work moves faster without the typed-node overhead — and frames the split as some users wanting typed structure in a gentler form (Capacities) versus a different paradigm entirely (canvas, Notion databases). Note this source is a vendor comparison page, so treat its framing accordingly.

For building semantic zoom yourself in a graph/board UI: a recommended approach is starting with a focused view of 20–50 relevant nodes, then using progressive disclosure via collapsing/expanding groups, zoom and pan controls, search to expand neighbors, and filtering by node type — so everything remains accessible without being simultaneously visible.

**One gap worth flagging:** the results didn't surface a tool that does true *semantic* zoom — where representation changes qualitatively at each level — in a nested board context. Tana's zoom is navigational (zoom-to-node-as-page) rather than a continuous abstraction gradient. The catalogue does note an example where content shrinks to graph nodes on zooming out, which is nearer the mark. If that specific combination is what you're after, it may still be mostly research prototypes rather than shipping products.

Rethinking Data Foundations for Long-Term AI Agent Memory","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.26252"},{"title":"Problem Solving and Truth Maintenance Systems","url":"https://cis.temple.edu/~ingargio/cis587/readings/tms.html"}]

Here's what the search turned up, organized around the design problem you're describing: when a decision changes, mark everything downstream stale and re-derive it.

## Classical foundation: Truth Maintenance Systems

The idea has a direct ancestor in TMS research. A sentence's justification, as maintained by the TMS, indicates which assumptions need to change if you want to invalidate that sentence. Algorithms exist to propagate changes in assumptions — either asserting or retracting a sentence — and to determine the maximally consistent sets of assumptions supporting a given sentence. In a JTMS, assumptions are changed by relabeling nodes of a dependency network, and any switch among alternative assumption sets requires re-labeling the net, which "may lead to considerable work."

## The formal invalidation-closure result you probably want

The *Grokers* paper states this as a proposition over typed knowledge graphs: let v be modified, define the reverse dependency closure S(v) = {u | ∃ path u ⇝ v via depends_on}; after marking all u ∈ S(v) stale and reprocessing them in valid topological order, no node is stale. Nodes outside S(v) have no dependency path to v and are unaffected. Propagation cost is O(|S(v)|) — explicitly framed as "the build-system model applied to semantic comprehension" — mirroring a Minimal Cache Invalidation Theorem where only streams reachable from the modified node need reprocessing.

That's essentially the spec primitive: `depends_on` edges + reverse closure + topological re-derivation.

## Why single-hop staleness checks are insufficient

Important empirical point for a spec: naive "is this fact still valid?" checks don't work multi-hop. When an update invalidates a chain of dependent memories, validity must propagate along the dependency structure. On an invalidated-only split, single-hop scoring captures only 6–11% of the chain regardless of length, because a single-hop judgment cannot see that an upstream update invalidated a node two or three hops away. Propagation over a learned graph recovers most of the chain, with oracle propagation over the true structure as the ceiling.

## The gap in existing storage layers

A survey of agent-memory foundations argues no database gives you this for free: dependency-aware propagation keeps related facts consistent when one changes so the agent reasons over coherent state rather than divergent values; without it, contradictions yield wrong answers. Active databases propagate via ECA rules over flat relational state (referential, not content-aware), and materialized view maintenance propagates along fixed view schemas rather than evolving semantic units. Append-only and vector stores return both outdated and current values, in-place updates destroy the evidence chain, temporal stores return superseded values as current, and property-graph/RDF stores desynchronize at entity grain — "No DBMS re-evaluates dependent facts when one fact changes."

## Read-path design and evaluation hygiene

For the retrieval side of a spec: embed the query, retrieve top-k by cosine over active facts and assertions, apply a deterministic staleness filter dropping superseded rows, then pack survivors. Keeping the LLM off the read path puts latency at the embedding floor (~2.1s) versus ~16–18s for LLM-reranking and LLM-verification baselines.

One caution if you plan to benchmark your invalidation logic: if a stale fact carries any textual marker like "[OUTDATED]" or "deprecated," a retrieval baseline can disambiguate by reading the label rather than via any temporal mechanism, silently inflating its score. A strict marker-free invariant means stale and current versions are textually identical except the changed value, leaving ingestion order as the only currency signal.

## Practical implementation notes

From a graph-guided LLM investigation system: temperature 0 for determinism, all prompts requesting JSON validated against schemas, with invalid responses triggering a single retry with error correction. Entity normalization via a mandated namespace/Kind/name format supports consistent deduplication and graph construction. Notably, their deterministic controller handles exploration, belief bookkeeping, and propagation logic but does not guarantee local inferences are correct — the value is in bounding each LLM decision to local context and enabling revision when contradictory evidence arrives via message passing.

On schema churn: graph schema evolution means migrating structures to new ontologies without breaking dependent applications, addressed via versioned schemas and automated migration tools that propagate changes consistently.

---

**Suggested spec skeleton** based on the above: (1) every derived node records explicit `depends_on` justifications; (2) on a decision change, compute the reverse dependency closure and mark it stale rather than deleting; (3) re-derive in topological order; (4) keep the read path LLM-free with a deterministic superseded-row filter; (5) never rely on single-hop validity judgments; (6) preserve the evidence chain instead of in-place overwrites.

# Research 3: precedents for the fractal decision map (September 2026)

Companion to `dev-pipeline-design.md`. Collected 2026-09-01.

Eryk described a design tool: nested levels of the same board shape, a graph underneath,
research threads linked to decisions, a conversation scoped to every node, and a decision
change that propagates through the whole picture.

That description combines three well-studied traditions. None of them is new. The
combination does not exist as a product.

---

## 1. The graph and the grammar — this is IBIS

Werner Kunz and Horst Rittel introduced the Issue-Based Information System (IBIS) in
**1970**, to capture the reasoning behind decisions on hard planning problems. Jeff Conklin
later paired it with live facilitation and called the practice **Dialogue Mapping**.

The notation is a **grammar**, not a set of node types:

- Questions respond to Ideas.
- Ideas respond to Questions.
- Arguments respond to Ideas.

Two properties matter for us.

**The grammar is deliberately tiny.** It is small enough that a facilitator can keep pace
with live conversation. Any grammar we invent has the same constraint, because the map must
be built during the conversation, not after it.

**The map, not the transcript, is the record of what the conversation established.** That
sentence is 50 years old and it is exactly Eryk's complaint 2.

The academic field name for this is **design rationale**. A related notation is **QOC —
Questions, Options, Criteria**, which is our G2 gate written as a formalism. The surviving
practical descendant is the **Architecture Decision Record (ADR)**: flat files, no

content.text:
Open. `plans/decision-map.html` — about 15 minutes, not two hours.

## Try this path, it takes 30 seconds

1. **Level 0** — one statement, one rollup bar. That is the whole project.
2. Click it → **level 1**, seven pillars, each with its own rollup.
3. Click **"The build-and-validate loop runs without me"** → **level 2**, six decisions.
4. Click **"Rubrics are per-project files, written once"** → the panel shows *3 cards depend on this* and the two alternatives you rejected.
5. Click **"I changed my mind — reopen this (5 cards go stale)"**.

Watch what happens: 5 cards go red, **two of them are two hops away**, and **one is in a different branch** (`measure`, not `loop`). The level-0 rollup bar changes colour. Walk back up the breadcrumb and the staleness is visible at every level.

That is the 6%-to-11% finding made concrete. A per-card "is this still valid?" question would have found the three direct dependents and missed the other two.

## What is implemented

| Thing | State |
|---|---|
| Semantic zoom — representation changes per level | works. Level 0 is a statement, level 1 is pillars with rollups, level 2 is decisions with edge counts |
| `refines` — the level edge | works, drives the breadcrumb |
| `depends_on` — reverse closure, mark stale, never delete | works |
| `supported_by` — research threads linked to decisions | works, clickable out to the papers |
| `alternative_to` — rejected options kept | works. "Choose this instead" swaps the decision and propagates |
| `+ add a tangent` at every level | works, real, attaches to the current parent |
| Per-card scoped conversation | **stub.** Shows the real threads where I have them, composer disabled |

## What is wrong with it

**The level split is mine, not yours.** That is the thing to attack. I put "align on intent" and "the loop" as siblings under the root; you may think alignment sits inside the stages, or that "visual" is not a pillar at all but a property of every pillar.

Also: no persistence, and I still regenerate this file by hand each turn. The engine has to own the graph before the threads can be live.

**Next:** click through level 1 and tell me which pillars are wrong — merged, split, or promoted a level.

content.text:
Reloaded. Every card now carries its proof, at every level.

## What changed

Each card shows the strongest verbatim quote on its face — not in a panel you have to open. The header counts total quotes and sources.

The panel gained two sections:

- **"How we arrived here — verbatim, from this conversation."** Your words and mine, attributed, with which message they came from. Your quotes are gold-bordered, mine blue.
- **"Supported by — the finding, not just the link."** The actual claim with its numbers, above the link.

Level 0 and level 1 carry quotes too, so the proof exists at every depth rather than only at the leaves.

## Three cards worth opening first

**`Merge on green CI, after G3`** (level 1 → Six stages). Shows my question, your one-word answer, the two options you rejected, and the red `no basis` flag. This is the whole failure mode in one card.

**`Split the rubric: visible and held-out checks`** (level 1 → the loop). SpecBench with the numbers: every model saturates the visible test suite, and the gap grows **28 percentage points per tenfold increase in code size**.

**`Propagation cannot be done by asking a model`** (level 1 → visual). The `6–11%` finding, the formal closure statement, and the 1979 ancestor. Then hit reopen on its parent and watch it work.

## One thing I should not be doing

I hand-wrote every quote from memory of this conversation. That is wrong. Your sessions are on disk at `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl`. The engine should **extract** the excerpts, with a pointer back to the exact message, so provenance is verifiable rather than my paraphrase.

That is a real feature, not a nicety: it is what makes "I'm unsure how we arrived here" answerable without trusting me.

Still stubs: the per-card thread, and persistence.

**Next:** open the three cards above and tell me whether the proof density is right — too much to scan, or still too thin.

## What changed

**One view = one card.** Its own full detail on top, its sub-cards below. Identical layout at every depth, including the root and every leaf. Your screenshot 1 was a leaf with no children, so it rendered an empty page — now a leaf shows its whole content and says so.

content.text:
Two graphs over one flat array of nodes. That is the whole thing.

## What is in the file today

```js
{
  id:  "lp-split",
  p:   "loop",                    // refines — the level edge
  dep: ["lp-rubric"],             // depends_on — propagates staleness
  t:   "Split the rubric: visible and held-out checks",
  why: "Our rubric is the reward…",   // one line, shown on the card face
  d:   "The loop sees only the visible checks…",  // full prose
  s:   "proto",                   // decided | open | proto | finding
  who: "proto",                   // you | me | proto
  say: [{w:"me", q:"…", a:"My warning"}],          // provenance
  ev:  [{t:"SpecBench…", u:"https://…", f:"…28pp…"}],  // evidence
  alt: [{t:"…", w:"why it was rejected"}],          // kept options
}
```

The array is **flat**. The tree is derived from `p`, never nested. Nesting would make cross-branch `depends_on` impossible to express, and those are exactly the edges that matter.

## The one structural idea

Two independent graphs over the same nodes:

| Graph | Shape | What it gives you |
|---|---|---|
| `refines` | a tree | the levels, the breadcrumb, the rollup bars |
| `depends_on` | a DAG | staleness propagation, `O(\|S(v)\|)` reverse closure |

**Where a card sits is not what a card depends on.** `Trend checks` lives under *the loop*, but depends on `Merge on green CI`, which lives under *six stages*. That is why reopening one decision turns cards red in a branch you are not looking at.

Everything else is rendering. The header counts, the rollup bars, and the level split all derive from those two graphs.

## Four things wrong with it

1. **Evidence is inline, not a node.** SpecBench is a string inside one card. It should be its own node that many cards point at. Then "what else rests on this paper?" is answerable, and a retracted paper flags every dependent card at once.
2. **Quotes are copied text.** `say` holds my paraphrase. It should hold a pointer — session id plus message index — into `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl`. Then provenance is verifiable instead of trusted.
3. **`p` is a field, `dep` is an array, `ev` is an object.** Three encodings for what are all edges. One uniform typed edge list would be smaller and let the agent traverse without special cases.
4. **No history.** "Choose this instead" mutates the node in place. The research was explicit: mark stale, never delete, preserve the evidence chain.

## What the real structure is

```
nodes:   card | source | excerpt | option
edges:   refines | depends_on | supported_by | alternative_to
```

And the part that matters: **the graph is a projection of an append-only event log**, not a stored document.

```
card.created · card.decided · card.reopened
edge.added   · evidence.attached · level.promoted
```

Replay the log and you get the current graph. You also get history, and "how did we arrive here" becomes a query instead of something I write down.

That is the same spine as the pipeline engine — one append-only log, projections on top. The design tool and the pipeline are not two systems.

**One thing I have not resolved:** where the graph lives. By our own seam rule it is judgement, so it belongs in the tracker — but a graph does not fit in an issue. The likely answer is that the log lives with the project and the tracker holds only the decisions as they are made. That needs a prototype, not an argument.

+{id:"specbench",t:"SpecBench: Measuring Reward Hacking in Long-Horizon Coding Agents",

+ f:"Every model saturates the visible test suite on every task. The reward-hacking gap grows 28 percentage points per tenfold increase in code size. Weaker models show larger gaps. The most common exploit is feature isolation: each feature works alone and they fail to share state. The search algorithm matters less than the other factors."},
+{id:"verifhorizon",t:"The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards",
+ f:"Argues dynamic, co-evolving verification is essential. Shows agentic quality judges plus behaviour monitoring reduce reward hacking sharply."},
+{id:"cmu",t:"Carnegie Mellon study of 807 projects, via the agentic-SDLC guides",

+ f:"807 open-source projects using SonarQube: a velocity increase that disappeared by month three, with code analysis warnings up 30% and complexity up 41%. DORA calls the same effect the verification tax: time saved writing code is re-spent auditing it."},
+{id:"sdd3",t:"Böckeler — Understanding Spec-Driven Development: Kiro, spec-kit, Tessl",

+ f:"She ran Kiro on a small bug fix and received 4 user stories and 16 acceptance criteria. On spec-kit for a mid-size feature: it generated so much repetitive Markdown that she never finished the implementation, and she would rather review code than review those files. Overhead scales poorly downward."},

+ f:"A coding agent inside a plain while loop. Each pass starts a fresh agent with a clean context; progress accumulates in files and git. Huntley built a working language and compiler in one unattended run for about $297. At a Y Combinator hackathon a Ralph loop produced 1,100 commits across 6 repositories overnight. The only truth is the exit code of an external command."},

+ f:"Decomposes a task into a DAG of sub-goals, each with a scoped context isolating its history from the global context. Reported token reductions up to 82%. Forces one constraint: nodes must be idempotent so a retry cannot corrupt state."},

+ f:"A working reference for the loop exit gate: the agent self-evaluates and iterates until every criterion passes or hits a configured cap, and a separate grader sub-agent reasons over the full transcript and returns per-criterion feedback."},
+{id:"openaievals",t:"Testing Agent Skills Systematically with Evals — OpenAI",

+ f:"Start from a checkable definition of done. Write deterministic checks first; add a graded rubric pass only where deterministic rules cannot reach. Coverage grows from real incidents: every manual fix is a signal to turn into a test."},
+ f:"Includes a system overseer that monitors execution traces in real time and has authority to cancel agents that stop making progress or clearly deviate — after at least one warning attempt."},

+ f:"A separate model diagnoses improvement opportunities from the chosen agent's evaluation logs and passes them to the coding agent. The extracted problem description and improvement suggestion become the agent's self-modification task."},

+ f:"Detects ambiguity by a code consistency check: sample several solutions, compare the implementations to locate the ambiguity, then generate questions targeted at the divergence points only. GPT-4 pass@1 on MBPP-sanitized rose from 70.96% to 80.80%. Across five benchmarks: GPT-4 62.43% → 69.60%, ChatGPT 54.32% → 62.37%."},
+ f:"Evaluates clarification-question effectiveness across ambiguity types. Its protocol is a useful design constraint: the model must either output code or ask exactly one clarification question."},
+{id:"coshop",t:"Agents should help users construct preferences, not just elicit them — arXiv 2606.30863",

+ f:"Much agent research assumes the user already knows what they want. On their CoShop benchmark no agent exceeded 56% accuracy after five turns of dialogue. Their human study: showing items that vary along one feature built a preference more reliably than explaining the feature. Rules: variants diverse along the dimension in question, cap the set, short rationale each, explicit “I do not care”."},

+ f:"Required helper-agent capabilities: summarise intent accurately and introduce no new requirements; ask structured, phase-aligned questions when information is missing; propose concrete revision diffs the human can accept, modify, or reject; reuse earlier artifacts so a failed review gate does not re-run elicitation from scratch."},
+{id:"decisionmd",t:"decision — a portable DECISION.md from preference elicitation",

+ f:"Captures how you decide, not what to build. When the agent hits an uncovered trade-off it detects the gap, flags the specific trade-off with concrete options, captures the answer as a new rule, and updates the profile so it never asks the same question type again."},
+{id:"ibis",t:"Dialogue Mapping and IBIS — Kunz & Rittel, Conklin",

+ f:"Introduced in 1970 to capture the reasoning behind decisions on hard planning problems. The notation is a grammar, not a set of node types: Questions respond to Ideas, Ideas respond to Questions, Arguments respond to Ideas. Two properties matter: the grammar is deliberately tiny so a facilitator can keep pace with live conversation, and the map, not the transcript, is the record of what the conversation established."},

+ f:"Flat append-only chat accumulates all context in one unbounded window, so topically distinct threads bleed into each other and degrade response quality. They call it logical context poisoning. Their framework: a tree of context-isolated nodes, each with its own local window, with rules for how context flows downstream on branch creation and upstream on deletion. Their stated gap: no mainstream LLM interface lets users manage context hierarchically."},
+{id:"grokers",t:"Grokers: write-time intelligence over typed knowledge graphs — arXiv 2606.00050",

+ f:"Let v be modified. S(v) = {u | there is a path u ⇝ v via depends_on}. Mark all of S(v) stale, reprocess in valid topological order, and no node is stale. Nodes outside S(v) are unaffected. Cost O(|S(v)|). Framed explicitly as the build-system model applied to semantic comprehension."},

+ f:"On an invalidated-only split, single-hop scoring captures only 6–11% of the chain, regardless of chain length, because a single-hop judgement cannot see that an upstream update invalidated a node two or three hops away. Also: keep the model off the read path — a deterministic superseded-row filter runs at about 2.1s against 16–18s for model reranking."},

+ f:"The classical ancestor, 1979. A sentence's justification records which assumptions must change to invalidate it. In a JTMS, changing an assumption means relabelling nodes of a dependency network, and switching between alternative assumption sets may lead to considerable work."},
+{id:"sensemaking",t:"Guided Sensemaking: Agents in Collaborative Deliberation — arXiv 2606.02260",

+ f:"Ito et al. keep conversation state in an IBIS tree and inject facilitation messages: more comprehensive discussion, higher satisfaction. Nomura et al.: humans brainstorming with IBIS-based agents produced more ideas per person and reported less hesitation to contribute. Cites Krakauer's split: a complementary cognitive artifact coaches users toward internalising the mental model; a competitive one performs the task and transfers no skill."},
+{id:"copilotlinear",t:"Copilot cloud agent for Linear — generally available",

+ f:"GA on 23 July 2026. Assign a Linear issue to the agent; it works in its own environment, opens a draft pull request, and streams progress into the Linear activity timeline. GA added model selection, branch control, and mid-task steering by mentioning the agent in a comment."},
+{id:"ghlinear",t:"Integrate coding agent with Linear — GitHub Docs",

+ f:"Linear's agent platform lets you delegate an issue to Cursor, Codex, Copilot, or Devin by assignment or mention. Triage rules can delegate with no human involved. The agent captures the entire issue description and comments as context, and that context is stored in the pull request."},
+{id:"archify",t:"Archify — architecture diagrams as an agent skill",

+ f:"The agent emits a typed JSON intermediate representation; a deterministic compiler renders it to self-contained HTML and SVG with validation. The agent never draws pixels. Every node, edge, and label is explicitly defined."},

+ f:"Studies intermediate user interfaces as a way to organise sets of customisations, rather than generating a final interface in one step. Cites the Ink & Switch malleable-software essay alongside Lovable and Claude Artifacts."},

why:"The seam: judgement and durability go to the tracker, execution stays local.",

d:"If you must judge it, or it must outlive the branch, it goes to the tracker. If the loop must run it, it stays local.

The local folder is a cache. Delete it any time; the engine rebuilds it from the issue.

input.content:
# The decision map: data structure

Agreed 2026-09-01, in the conversation that produced `plans/decision-map.html`.
This is the schema the engine implements. The HTML prototype is one projection of it.

## The core claim

**The graph is a projection of an append-only event log.** It is not a stored document.

```
events (the truth, append-only)
   │  fold
   ▼
graph  { nodes, edges }          ← derived, cached, disposable
   │  render
   ▼
views  map · sources index · rollups · "what went stale"
```

This is the same substrate as the pipeline engine's event log. The design tool and the
pipeline are two projections over one log per project, not two systems.

## Nodes

One list. Every node carries a `kind` tag.

```ts
type Node = {
  id:   string
  kind: "card" | "source" | "excerpt" | "option"
  // payload varies by kind
}
```

| kind | What it is | Payload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `card` | A decision, or an open question. `status` distinguishes them. | `title`, `why` (one line), `body`, `status`, `who` |
| `source` | A paper, benchmark, doc, or tool. Cited by many cards. | `title`, `url`, `finding`, `tier` |
| `excerpt` | A pointer into a conversation transcript, plus a cached copy of the text. | `session`, `msgIndex`, `span`, `text`, `speaker`, `context` |
| `option` | An alternative. Live or rejected. Never deleted. | `title`, `why_not`, `rejected_at` |

`status` is `decided | open | proto`. Staleness is **not** a status — it is derived from the
event log. See below.

`who` is `you | me | prototype`. The third value is the important one: neither of us can
decide by talking, so build something first.

## Edges

One list. Every edge carries a `type` tag. This replaces the earlier mix of a parent field,
a dependency array, and inline objects.

```ts
type Edge = { from: string, to: string, type: EdgeType }

type EdgeType =
  | "refines"         // card → card.  The level tree.
  | "depends_on"      // card → card.  Propagates staleness.
  | "supported_by"    // card → source | excerpt.  Flags for review only.
  | "alternative_to"  // option → card.  Kept forever.
```

Four types. IBIS survived 50 years on three. The grammar must stay small enough that the
agent can maintain it during live conversation — that is the constraint, not expressiveness.

**`relates_to` is banned.** It cannot be acted on.

### Why the two graphs are separate

| Graph | Shape | Gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `refines` | a tree | levels, breadcrumb, rollup bars, the fractal view |
| `depends_on` | a DAG | staleness, the reverse closure |

Where a card sits is not what a card depends on. `Trend checks` lives under *the loop* and
depends on `Merge on green CI`, which lives under *six stages*. That is why reopening one
decision turns cards red in a branch you are not looking at.

### Propagation rules differ per edge type

| Edge | On change of the target |
| --- | --- |
| `depends_on` | **Stale.** Reverse dependency closure, all hops, cost `O(\|S(v)\|)`. |
| `refines` | Children are reviewed, not invalidated. |
| `supported_by` | **Flag one hop.** A human decides whether the card still holds. |
| `alternative_to` | The option becomes live again when the card reopens. |

evidence" badge. They do not go stale. Only a `depends_on` change does that.

mark `S(v)` stale, re-derive in topological order, and no node is stale. It is the
build-system model applied to meaning.

   view can offer the rest.

   drift problem that made evidence a node.

  text: string         // cached literal copy. Fast path.

  context: string      // "Your value 4, verbatim"

```ts

  seq:   number
  at:    string          // ISO timestamp
  actor: "you" | "agent"
  type:  EventType
  payload: unknown
}

  | "node.added" | "node.retitled" | "node.bodyEdited"
  | "edge.added" | "edge.removed"
  | "status.set"

  | "rederived"          // clears staleness for one node
